newsitem.title: JAPAN: GE chairman urges Japan firms to cut weak units.
newsitem.headline: GE chairman urges Japan firms to cut weak units.

text.p: The chairman of giant U.S. conglomerate General Electric (GE) admonished Japanese corporate managers on Wednesday for being reluctant to sell off weak and unpromising subsidiaries.

Speaking at the 50th anniversary of the Kansai Association of Corporate Executives in Osaka, the commercial hub of western Japan, John Welch also suggested that Japanese managers speed up their decisions.

"Americans tend to think in terms of weeks and months, while Japanese take years and decades," Welch said in his address. "Patience was good for much of the 70s and early 80s but in the 90s, things have changed."
He said Japan's virtue for patience and paternalism had now become an impediment, and urged managers to discard the notion of disloyalty to their employees when detaching weak subsidiaries.

"It may be time for Japan to consider looking into its traditional business practices and to start rationalising -- selling off smaller and weaker business or perhaps even merging them with stronger ones," Welch said.
"Selling weaker businesses is not betraying the employees," Welch said.
"Forming subsidiaries and putting them to sleep in corners makes no sense," Welch said. "It is the manager's job to create an atmosphere where every employee is happy."

Welch cited GE's successful experience in selling off its air-conditioning business to a strong rival in the field in the early 1980s. He spoke similarly of the trade of GE's television business with French firm Thomson SA's that of medical equipment.
GE's conglomerate includes U.S. television network NBC which broadcast the Atlanta Summer Olympic games.
Many Japanese managers responded to Welch's comments by saying Japan's system of lifetime employment posed different problems.

To this, Welch said: "Restructuring weak business into stronger ones does not mean throwing away lifetime employment. It means putting people out of dead business and giving them a chance to grow in live business."

At a news conference later in the day, Welch was asked whether he thought Japan's competitiveness abroad was being eroded by long years of recession and the "hollowing out" of domestic industry through movement of production facilities to other countries.
"The last thing you have to be worried about is Japan's (international) competitiveness," Welch said.

"In the last 12 months, Japanese firms have become 30 percent more competitive. And to stay competitive in the face of the U.S. dollar moving from 360 to 80 yen (in the last two decades) is one of the greatest achievements in business history."
